title: How to Use a Garlic Press for a Quick Garlic-Chili Oil
meta_description: Learn how to make spicy garlic-chili oil in minutes using a garlic press. A simple, flavorful recipe for drizzling over pizza, pasta, and more.
html:
There is nothing quite like the aroma of sizzling garlic hitting hot oil, especially when it is spiked with dried chili flakes. While mincing garlic by hand yields a rustic texture, it can be tedious and leaves your fingers smelling for hours. If you want maximum flavor with minimal effort, making a garlic press chili oil is the way to go. Using a reliable tool like a sturdy stainless and silicone Garlic Press allows you to skip the knife work entirely, getting you to that delicious sizzle much faster.

Why a Garlic Press Creates Better Infusions

When you make garlic press chili oil, the physics of the tool actually help the flavor profile. A knife leaves you with distinct chunks that take time to break down and soften in the heat. A press, however, forces the cloves through small holes, creating a fine paste and releasing the essential oils immediately. This means the garlic mingles with the fat instantly, infusing the oil with a stronger, more pungent taste in a fraction of the time.

The Garlic Press is specifically designed to handle this pressure without bending, ensuring every bit of the clove is utilized. Because sturdy stainless and silicone garlic presses that mince, crush, and clean up easy are so efficient, you don't need to wrestle with the cloves. You get a consistent texture every time, which is crucial for an oil that coats your food evenly rather than sitting in pools.

Gathering Your Ingredients

You don't need a long shopping list to pull this off, but quality matters. Since there are so few ingredients, each one plays a starring role.

The Oil: Use a neutral oil with a high smoke point, such as grapeseed, canola, or avocado oil. You want something that won't burn when the garlic hits the pan. Avoid extra virgin olive oil for the cooking process, as its low smoke point can make the oil taste bitter at high heat. Save the good olive oil for drizzling over the finished dish if you wish.

The Heat: Standard crushed red pepper flakes work perfectly for a classic look and taste. However, if you want to get fancy, try Korean gochugaru flakes for a slightly sweeter, fruitier heat, or Aleppo pepper for a milder, more complex kick.

Step-by-Step Instructions

This process comes together in less than ten minutes, but you need to pay attention to the heat to prevent burning the garlic.

  1. Prep the Garlic: Peel your cloves. Place them into the chamber of your Garlic Press. Squeeze the handles together to force the garlic through the holes directly into a small heat-proof bowl or ramekin. You want roughly 3 to 4 cloves for every half cup of oil, depending on your spice tolerance.
  2. Heat the Pan: Pour your neutral oil into a small skillet or saucepan. Turn the heat to medium-low. You want the oil hot enough to sizzle gently, but not smoking.
  3. Infuse the Flavors: Add your garlic paste to the oil immediately. Stir constantly with a wooden spoon or silicone spatula. The garlic will bubble vigorously. Let it cook for about 1 minute until it becomes pale golden and fragrant.
  4. Add the Heat: Sprinkle in your chili flakes. Stir well to combine. Let the mixture simmer for another 30 to 60 seconds. The oil will turn a beautiful reddish-orange. Remove the pan from the heat immediately once the garlic is a deep golden brown. If it turns black, it will be bitter.
  5. Cool and Store: Let the oil cool completely in the pan. Once cool, pour it into a clean glass jar or bottle. Seal it tight.

Ways to Use Your Chili Oil

Now that you have your homemade garlic press chili oil, the possibilities are endless. Drizzle it over pizzas for an instant upgrade, or stir it into mayonnaise to create a spicy sandwich spread. It is fantastic over roasted vegetables, particularly broccoli or cauliflower, and adds a punch to a simple bowl of ramen or noodles.

My favorite way to use it is simply as a dipping sauce for crusty bread. It is also excellent for finishing a steak; spoon a little over the meat right after it comes off the grill to let the residual heat wake up the aromatics.

Cleaning Up

One of the biggest complaints about garlic tools is the cleaning process. Fortunately, the Garlic Press mentioned here is designed to be easy to maintain. Many models feature a built-in cleaning tool or a reverse mechanism that pushes the stuck skins out. If yours doesn't, simply run it under warm water immediately after use; the water will soften the remaining garlic, and a quick scrub with a brush will have it looking brand new.

FAQ

Do I have to peel the garlic before using the press?

Most traditional presses require you to peel the cloves first. While some premium models claim to press unpeeled cloves, peeling them usually results in a smoother paste and less strain on the tool, ensuring you get the best texture for your oil.

How long does this chili oil last?

Because this recipe contains fresh garlic water content, it should be stored in the refrigerator and used within one week for safety and best flavor. If you want a shelf-stable oil, you need to dry the garlic completely before infusing it or use dried garlic granules.

Can I use fresh chilies instead of flakes?

Absolutely. If you have fresh jalapeños or Thai bird's eye chilies, you can mince them finely. However, fresh chilies contain water that can cause the oil to splatter more violently when added to the pan, so be careful and lower the heat slightly if you go this route.
